question.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-4x(t)-2x(t)^{3}+y(t)^{2} \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)-3y(t)^{3}+x(t)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
question.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2} \\ -3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=-4-6{x}^{2} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-4x-2{x}^{3}+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-3y-3{y}^{3}+{x}^{2})=-3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-4-6{x}^{2} & 2y \\ 2x & -3-9{y}^{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Now evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium at ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get 

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-4-6(0)^{2} & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & -3-9(0)^{2}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & -3\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-4-\lambda  & 0 \\ 0 & -3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (-4-\lambda )(-3-\lambda ) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-3,\text{ }-4.$

Finally, since we have two real and negative eigenvalues, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{sink}.$
